what: GXO Logistics runs warehouses for other companies. A retailer or manufacturer hands over its distribution centres and GXO operates them: receiving goods, storing them, picking orders, packing and shipping, increasingly with robots and automation. It was spun out of XPO to be a pure contract logistics business.
customers: Large retailers, e-commerce companies, consumer goods manufacturers, industrial firms and aerospace companies, mostly in Europe and North America, on contracts that typically run several years.
money: Operating warehouses and distribution for customers, charged per unit handled or on a cost-plus basis.
moat: Once GXO runs a customer’s distribution network, moving it is a severe operational risk: a botched transition means goods not reaching shops. Contracts are long and renew at high rates. The automation is the real differentiator — GXO deploys robotics across many sites, which spreads the engineering cost over a scale that an individual retailer running its own warehouse cannot match.
risks: Margins are very thin: $136.0M of net income on $13.8B of revenue, and the shares trade at about 46 times earnings as a result.
Debt of about $5.9B against $854.0M of cash is substantial, raised partly for the Wincanton acquisition.
Labour is the main cost and warehouse wages have risen sharply; contracts cannot always be repriced as quickly.
Revenue depends on customers’ volumes, so a consumer slowdown reduces the units handled and therefore the revenue, without reducing the fixed cost of the site.
Heavy exposure to the United Kingdom and Europe adds currency translation risk and exposure to weaker European consumer demand.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $7.9B in 2021 to $13.2B in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $13.8B.
Outsourcing warehouse operations is a structural trend: companies increasingly conclude that running distribution is not their core skill.
Automation raises throughput per worker, which both improves margin and makes GXO harder to replace once installed.
Seventeen analysts average a $72.53 target, about 35% above the current price.
Contracts are long and renewal rates are high, so the revenue base is far more predictable than the thin margin suggests.
watch: Organic revenue growth and new business won. Acquisitions have driven much of the reported growth; whether the underlying business is winning contracts on its own is the honest measure.
view: Contract logistics is a business with excellent customer retention and terrible margins, and both facts come from the same place. The retention is excellent because moving a distribution network is genuinely dangerous — a failed transition means empty shelves — so customers renew almost automatically. The margins are terrible because the service is sold to sophisticated buyers who know roughly what it costs, and GXO keeps about one percent of the revenue that passes through it.

At 46 times earnings that one percent looks alarming, and it is the reason the headline multiple is meaningless here. The business should be judged on EV/EBITDA, where it trades at about 15 times, and on whether the automation story is real. That is the genuine question: GXO’s argument is that deploying robotics across hundreds of sites spreads the engineering cost in a way no single retailer can match, which both raises throughput per worker and makes the operation harder to take back in-house. If that holds, margins should drift upward over years and the thin margin becomes a feature rather than a flaw.

The risk I would weigh most heavily is operating leverage in reverse. A warehouse has a largely fixed cost base; revenue depends on the units a customer actually ships. In a consumer slowdown the units fall and the costs do not, and with a one percent net margin there is nothing to absorb it. Add $5.9 billion of debt, much of it from the Wincanton acquisition, and heavy exposure to a weak European consumer, and the downside case is not hard to construct.

What I would want separated out is how much of the growth from $7.9 billion to $13.2 billion was bought and how much was won. Acquisitive logistics companies have a long history of looking like growth stories while the underlying business merely treads water. The seventeen analysts at $72.53 are underwriting the automation thesis and a European recovery. I think the automation thesis is probably right and will take longer than anyone expects, which makes this a reasonable thing to own patiently and a poor thing to own in a hurry.
bull: Automation lifts margin across a growing site base while outsourcing keeps bringing new networks in, and a thin-margin business becomes a merely low-margin one at much larger scale.
bear: A consumer slowdown cuts the units flowing through fixed-cost warehouses, wage inflation outruns contract repricing, and a 1% margin has nothing to absorb either against $5.9 billion of debt.
